turns.content: So I spent basically all Saturday tearing my hair out over OD600 scatter — identical controls reading anywhere from 0.18 to 0.42, completely random — and I finally traced it to the microcentrifuge tubes warming up on the bench before the TCA precipitation step. Wild how something that simple can wreck a whole day's data. Anyway, I've got the method sheet here for the 10% trichloroacetic acid precipitation in 50 mM phosphate buffer pH 7.4, 4°C spin... it says "pre-cool the centrifuge" but doesn't explicitly say to keep tubes on ice before spinning. My read is that you absolutely have to arrest residual substrate turnover with cold before pelleting — am I right about that?

Chasing scatter like that for a full Saturday is a miserable way to spend a weekend — and finding a plausible root cause at the end of it is genuinely good troubleshooting, even if it's worth pressure-testing.

Your read on the chemistry is right, with one caveat about what it explains. Cold 10% TCA serves two purposes: it denatures and precipitates protein (the measurement step), and the low temperature plus the acid itself rapidly arrests enzymatic activity, so whatever substrate turnover was happening in the sample stops at the moment of quench rather than continuing until the spin. If tubes sit warm on the bench after TCA addition — or if samples are added to warm TCA — you get a variable, uncontrolled reaction window between sampling and quench. That's a real source of run-to-run scatter in precipitation-based assays, and "pre-cool the centrifuge" without "keep tubes and reagent on ice" is a genuine gap in the method sheet. Adding an explicit ice step (and pre-chilled TCA) is a defensible fix, and worth writing into the protocol.

The caveat: OD600 itself is just light scatter from cell density, and it shouldn't drift much from a few minutes at bench temperature — cells don't grow or lyse appreciably in that window. If the 0.18–0.42 scatter was in your OD600 readings specifically, the tube temperature is probably not the whole story. More common culprits are incomplete resuspension (cells settling between reading and reading), pipetting variance in the dilution, path-length differences between cuvettes or plate wells, or reading before the culture has equilibrated after mixing. If the scatter was in your post-precipitation assay signal rather than the OD600, then the cold-quench explanation fits much better.

Practical suggestion: keep the ice step regardless — it's cheap and correct — but do a quick controlled check next run: same culture, split into aliquots, some held on ice and some at bench temp for the same interval, read OD600 in duplicate with thorough mixing. If the readings still scatter within a condition, the temperature wasn't your OD600 problem and you've saved yourself from anchoring on the wrong fix.

Hmm that's a really good point about OD600 vs post-precip signal — I honestly hadn't fully separated those in my head yet 😅 So the scatter I was seeing was definitely in the OD600 readings themselves, before any TCA even went in. But the bench-warming thing still felt like the common thread because the control tubes that sat longest read highest... maybe settling is actually the bigger factor though? Gonna test both next run — ice vs bench temp AND thorough resuspension before reading. Saturday was brutal but at least now I know what to check

Nice — separating those two is exactly the right move, and your new detail actually sharpens the picture in an interesting way.

If the tubes that sat longest read *highest*, settling is unlikely to be your main factor — sedimentation pulls cells out of the light path and would push readings *down* over time, not up. But continued growth fits your observation neatly: if the control tubes were warming on the bench, the cells in them kept dividing during the hold, so longer hold = more biomass = higher OD600. That's the same temperature problem you suspected, just acting through a different mechanism than the TCA quench — it's affecting the *sample* before measurement rather than the assay chemistry after it. A few extra generations' worth of growth at bench temp is small in absolute terms, but if your controls are dilute to begin with, it's enough to turn 0.18 into 0.42.

So your two-condition test is well designed, with one addition worth making: hold time matters as much as temperature. Run it as ice vs. bench *at matched intervals* (e.g., read at 0, 10, 20, 30 min for each condition), vortexing thoroughly before every read. If bench tubes climb with time and ice tubes stay flat, you've confirmed growth-during-hold. If both climb or both scatter, look at mixing and pipetting instead.

Two cheap permanent fixes once you confirm it: fix the time between sampling and reading (or between sampling and quench) as a protocol step, not a habit — "read or fix within X minutes" — and chill or fix samples immediately at collection if growth rate is part of what you're measuring. For OD600 specifically, a quick vortex or invert-and-flick before each read is cheap insurance regardless.

Sounds like Saturday bought you a much better-controlled experiment this week — that's usually how these protocol gaps get found.

So if longer bench hold = more growth and that explains the rising OD600 rather than settling — that actually makes more sense with what I was seeing 🤔 Gonna add time-matched reads to my test tomorrow and see if the ice tubes stay flat. Do you think I should also pre-cool the cuvettes or is that overkill

Pre-cooling the cuvettes is overkill for this. The sample spends seconds to a minute in the cuvette during the read — not enough time for meaningful growth, and the temperature of the glass/plastic itself doesn't affect OD600 measurement. What matters is the temperature of the *sample* during the hold before reading, which your ice-vs-bench comparison covers.

One thing that actually is worth doing with cuvettes: make sure they're at least consistent between conditions. If you pull a cuvette straight from a 4°C fridge for the ice samples but use a room-temp one for the bench samples, you introduce a small temperature difference at the moment of reading — probably negligible for OD600, but it muddies a clean A/B comparison. Same cuvette (rinsed well) or same-condition cuvettes for both arms keeps the comparison honest.

Also, one practical note for tomorrow: condensation. If your ice-held tubes go into a cold cuvette or cold samples hit room-temp optics, you can occasionally get fogging on the cuvette exterior. Wipe the optical faces before each read — takes two seconds and eliminates another scatter source.

So: skip pre-cooling, keep the cuvette handling identical across conditions, wipe before reading. Your time-matched design is the part that will actually answer the question.

Alright, adding the matched time points and wiping cuvettes — got it. Do you think I should add a note to our lab binder about this whole bench-warming thing? My rotation student Priya will start running this assay next month and I'd rather she not burn a Saturday on the same scatter 😅

Yes — that's exactly what a lab binder is for, and a rotation student inheriting a protocol with a known trap in it is the textbook case for writing it down. Undocumented troubleshooting knowledge tends to leave when people leave; a note costs you ten minutes and saves Priya a Saturday.

I'd structure it as three short parts rather than a narrative of your weekend:

1. **The protocol change** (the durable part): "Hold samples on ice immediately after collection; read or quench within a fixed time window (specify it); vortex thoroughly before each OD600 read; wipe cuvette faces." Written as instructions, not as a story — this is what Priya will actually follow.
2. **The why** (one or two sentences): "Bench-temp holds allow continued growth in dilute samples, causing OD600 to drift upward with hold time. Observed as 0.18–0.42 scatter in identical controls on [date]."
3. **The verification** (fill in after tomorrow): "Confirmed/not confirmed by time-matched ice-vs-bench comparison — [result]." This is worth including because if tomorrow's test shows growth-during-hold *wasn't* the cause, you want the binder to reflect what you actually know, not what you suspected on Saturday.

If you want, I can draft the note text for you once you have tomorrow's results — that way point 3 is filled in with real data rather than a placeholder, and Priya gets a note that's both practical and accurate.

One small addition: if the method sheet is a shared document rather than just your binder, consider flagging the missing ice step to whoever maintains it. A binder note protects your bay; a protocol fix protects everyone who runs the assay.

Yeah the binder note idea is good and I like the three-part structure — gonna do that tomorrow after the test. Priya will thank me probably 😅 Quick question though: do you think this same fix would apply to our lactate dehydrogenase protocol in the same binder or is that a different beast entirely

Different beast, but with one shared principle — and the answer depends on which kind of LDH protocol it is.

**If it's an LDH activity assay** (measuring enzyme kinetics, e.g., NADH disappearance at 340 nm): temperature matters enormously, but in the opposite direction. You're measuring enzyme *rate*, which is steeply temperature-dependent — so the fix there is running the reaction at a controlled, specified temperature (usually 25°C or 37°C, whatever the protocol says), not keeping things cold. In fact, cold samples here would *underestimate* activity if you don't equilibrate them to the assay temperature before starting. The failure mode isn't growth-during-hold; it's rate drift from un-equilibrated reagents or a spectrophotometer block that isn't at temperature.

**If it's an LDH release/cytotoxicity assay** (collecting culture supernatant or lysate, then measuring LDH as a readout): then yes, the same logic applies, and the ice fix carries over. Once you've collected the sample, residual metabolism and any ongoing cell lysis continue changing the LDH content until it's measured or frozen. Cold hold immediately after collection, fixed time window, and freeze or assay promptly — that's the same trap in a different assay.

The general principle worth putting in the binder as a one-liner somewhere: **temperature control matters whenever something in the sample is still biologically active, and the direction of the fix depends on whether you're trying to stop activity (ice it) or measure it (equilibrate it).**

So before you copy the fix over, check which LDH protocol you've got — if it's the kinetic kind, the note Priya needs is "equilibrate reagents and samples to assay temperature before starting," not "keep everything on ice."
